content: All members of the Guideline Development Group (GDG) and external contributors were required to complete a standard World Health Organization (WHO) Declaration of Interest (DOI) form prior to participating in the guideline development process or attending related meetings. The WHO Steering Group reviewed all submitted DOI forms before finalizing invitations for experts to join the guideline development process. If any conflicts of interest were declared, the Steering Group assessed their severity to determine whether they could compromise the expert’s ability to provide objective judgment during the guideline development and recommendation formulation process. To ensure consistency, the Steering Group applied the criteria outlined in the WHO Handbook for Guideline Development to evaluate the severity of conflicts of interest for each expert. All findings from the DOI forms were managed on a case-by-case basis in accordance with WHO DOI guidelines and communicated to the experts. If a conflict of interest was deemed insignificant and unlikely to affect the credibility of the guideline development process, the expert was only required to disclose the conflict openly at the beginning of the GDG meeting, with no further action taken. Annex 4 provides a summary of the declared interests of the experts and details on how any conflicts of interest were managed by the WHO Steering Group. During the WHO Technical Consultation, the GDG discussed the draft recommendations prepared by the WHO Steering Group. In addition to evaluating the scientific evidence and its quality, the GDG considered factors such as values and preferences, the balance between benefits and harms, cost/resource implications, equity, acceptability, and feasibility when formulating the final recommendation. The GDG relied on their experience and opinions, supported by evidence from the literature where available, to assess values, preferences, and cost/resource implications. These considerations were documented and synthesized using evidence-to-decision tables. The final wording and strength of the recommendation were determined by consensus, defined as agreement by at least three-quarters of the participants. No GDG members expressed strong opposition to the final recommendation or its accompanying remarks. Before the Technical Consultation, the WHO Steering Group prepared a draft evidence summary and recommendation document, which was made available to participants two weeks prior to the meeting. During the meeting, the draft recommendation was revised based on participants’ deliberations and feedback. After the meeting, the WHO Steering Group prepared a draft of the full guideline document, incorporating revisions that accurately reflected the GDG’s discussions and decisions. This draft was sent electronically to GDG members for further comments before being submitted to the External Review Group (ERG) for peer review. The draft guideline and recommendation document were sent to four ERG members for peer review. The WHO Steering Group carefully evaluated the feedback from the peer reviewers for potential inclusion in the final guideline document. After the Technical Consultation and peer review processes were completed, any further modifications made by the Steering Group were limited to correcting factual errors and improving language clarity. The evidence supporting the recommendation was derived from a single systematic review, which served as the evidence base for the guideline. This systematic review included two randomized controlled trials (RCTs) conducted in eight African countries, involving a total of 684 women with simple obstetric urinary fistula. Both trials compared shorter and longer durations of postoperative bladder catheterization. The longer duration was 14 days in both trials, while the shorter duration was 10 days in one trial and 7 days in the other. The primary outcomes assessed were fistula repair breakdown and cure, with outcomes confirmed using dye tests. Five critical outcomes were identified for evaluating the length of postoperative bladder catheterization, but maternal satisfaction with care was not reported in any of the studies. Four additional outcomes were classified as important, but the cost of care was not reported in any of the studies. The evidence base did not indicate significant differences in adverse clinical outcomes between shorter and longer durations of postoperative bladder catheterization. However, shorter durations were associated with greater convenience for women, reduced discomfort, and a lower likelihood of complications related to catheterization. The overall quality of evidence was rated as low to moderate for critical outcomes, primarily due to imprecision in effect estimates caused by the rarity of events and wide confidence intervals. The GDG recommended a shorter duration of bladder catheterization (7 to 10 days) as an alternative to longer durations for women in the postoperative period following surgical repair of simple obstetric urinary fistula. This recommendation was based on the balance of benefits, including improved patient comfort, reduced risk of catheter-associated infections, and decreased demand for health services. The GDG acknowledged the uncertainty in outcomes for shorter versus longer durations but emphasized the potential benefits of shorter catheterization, such as faster recovery and reintegration into daily life. The GDG identified several research gaps, including the need to evaluate the effectiveness of bladder catheterization for less than 7 days, the applicability of shorter durations for complex fistula cases, and the cost-effectiveness of shorter versus longer durations. Additional research priorities included assessing strategies to reduce the incidence of obstetric fistula at the country level and developing community-based interventions for prevention.
